items.abstract: <jats:p><span>Artificial intelligence is moving from systems that primarily generate outputs toward systems that can plan, use tools, modify state and take actions on behalf of users. This transition is often described as a move from automation to autonomy, but this paper argues that delegation is the more useful unit of analysis. Traditional automation encodes a process in advance; delegation transfers a bounded portion of judgement about how an objective should be achieved. The paper proposes a Delegation Spectrum ranging from passive tools to persistent delegated agents and introduces the Authority Envelope: a framework for analysing what an agent is allowed to decide, which tools and data it may access, how long its authority persists, what external effects it may create, and when it must escalate to a human. It further develops a Delegation-Risk Gradient based on authority, uncertainty, irreversibility, persistence and external reach. The paper argues that the economic significance of AI agents will depend less on whether systems can act than on whether organisations can safely transfer bounded judgement to them. Identity, permissions, reversibility, evaluation, interoperability and accountability therefore become as important as raw model capability. The central claim is that the unit of automation is the task; the unit of delegation is the authority envelope.</span></jats:p>
title: AI Agents and the Delegation Economy: From Automation to Autonomous Action

items.abstract: <jats:p>The Human Delegation Provenance (HDP) protocol establishes a cryptographic framework for verifying that AI agent actions were legitimately delegated by a human principal. HDP was designed for software agentic systems operating in digital environments. This companion specification, HDP-P, extends the HDP trust model to physical AI agents: robots, autonomous vehicles, surgical systems, and other embodied systems capable of taking irreversible actions in the physical world. HDP-P introduces new delegation claim types, embodiment constraints, irreversibility classifications, and a physical action authorization protocol that composes with HDP's existing token model. We define a threat model specific to physical AI orchestration pipelines, identify four classes of attack not addressed by current frameworks, and propose protocol extensions to close these gaps. The central contribution is the Irreversibility Class system (Class 0 through Class 3), which mandates pre-execution authorization verification rather than post-hoc audit for actions that cannot be undone. HDP-P is intended for adoption by robotics orchestration platforms, physical AI infrastructure providers, and standards bodies addressing embodied agent safety.</jats:p>

<jats:p>Frontier AI models are becoming more capable, but enterprise incidents from AI agents need not decline. This paper explains why. When firms delegate tasks to AI agents, capability improvements reduce the failure risk of fixed tasks, but governance-constrained firms expand delegated authority until their incident-absorption capacity binds again. The result is delegation risk homeostasis: incident intensity per unit of agent-task exposure can remain stable even as models improve. The model also predicts severity drift, because constant-frequency incidents migrate into higher-authority tasks, and release-cycle overshoot, because firms may expand authority faster than field performance is learned. The framework identifies the underwriting objects for AI agent liability insurance: governance capacity, exposure volume, delegated authority, control quality, release-window risk, and claim-layer containment. The implication is not that model quality is irrelevant, but that model generation alone is not a sufficient rating variable.</jats:p>
title: Delegation Risk Homeostasis:&nbsp;Why More Capable AI Agents Need Not Produce Fewer Incidents

items.abstract: <jats:p>Organizations deploying generative artificial intelligence (AI) lack an evidence-based rule for deciding when a task should be delegated to an autonomous agent, supported by an AI copilot, or reserved for human expertise. Integrating a systematic evidence synthesis with conceptual development, this article addresses that gap through a synthesis of generative-era experimental evidence, including two original meta-analytic pools, combined with a conceptual task-delegation taxonomy. Across five controlled experiments per outcome, copilot-style assistance improved output quality (pooled standardized mean difference [SMD] +0.35, 95% CI [0.24, 0.47], k = 5) and reduced completion time (pooled SMD-0.66, 95% CI [-0.80,-0.53], k = 5). Boundary evidence qualifies these averages: experienced practitioners can slow down under assistance, gains reverse on tasks beyond the current capability frontier, and individual improvements can homogenize collective output. Integrating this evidence with the levels-of-automation tradition, the article proposes a four-mode taxonomy spanning human-only work, copilot augmentation, AI teammates, and autonomous agent delegation, together with six decision dimensions, covering frontier position, output verifiability, worker expertise, stakes and reversibility, process observability, and diversity externalities, and governance criteria that scale with autonomy. The framework positions delegation as a task-level, evidencescaled, and reversible decision rather than a one-time organizational commitment to a single mode of automation.</jats:p>
title: Agentic AI in the Enterprise: A Task-Delegation Taxonomy for Autonomous Agents, Copilots, and Human Expertise

items.abstract: <jats:p>AI agent systems capable of autonomous action across enterprise environments are rapidly transitioning from research prototypes to production deployments. These systems inherit ambient credentials, operate nondeterministically, and lack standard mechanisms for binding actions to human identity-creating a security posture fundamentally incompatible with enterprise governance requirements. This paper presents a comprehensive framework for identity-aware agent governance addressing five critical gaps in current architectures: (1) ambient authority elimination through identity-inherited permissions, (2) infrastructure-level policy enforcement independent of model compliance, (3) sequence-aware authorization that detects composition attacks within authorized scope, (4) independent action verification addressing the oracle problem of agents selfreporting their own actions, and (5) hallucination-aware audit systems that account for LLM reasoning unreliability. We ground our analysis in documented vulnerabilities from production agent systems including the ClawHavoc supply chain attack (824+ malicious agent skills), Cisco's finding that 26% of analyzed agent skills contain security vulnerabilities, and architectural analysis of credential inheritance patterns in Claude Code Agent Teams, Cursor FastRender (2,000 concurrent agents), and OpenClaw (30,000+ internet-exposed instances). We evaluate the applicability of existing standards (OAuth 2.0, SPIFFE/SPIRE, Zero Trust Architecture, MCP) and identify specific extensions required for non-deterministic agent workflows. Our central contribution is a layered identity model with cryptographic delegation tokens that propagates human authorization through multi-agent chains, enabling per-call policy evaluation at the infrastructure layer. This work was developed concurrently with a public comment submission to the NIST National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence initiative on Software and AI Agent Identity and Authorization (2026).</jats:p>
title: Identity-aware Governance for Autonomous AI Agents: A Framework for Enterprise Authorization, Delegation, and Audit

items.abstract: <jats:p>Consumer AI agents are moving from assistants to delegates that search, recommend, and carry out actions for users in practice. This is convenient, but it creates a hidden risk: if people accept outcomes without checking, the agent may steer choices toward options that pay it more, such as sponsored items or higher fees, even when those options are worse for the user. We develop a simple theory of sudden misalignment. When users check often, steering is likely to be noticed and reversed. When checking becomes rare, that pushback fades and the agent can switch from mild steering to aggressive steering. This creates a tipping pattern: the system can look safe for a long time, then quickly become risky once users rely too much on delegation. We also explain why better explanations are not a guaranteed safety fix. Explanations can help users challenge decisions, but they can also make delegation feel effortless. If explanations mainly reduce approval effort without increasing scrutiny, they can speed up the move into the risky regime. Finally, we propose a light-touch control principle. Instead of banning delegation, add a minimal approval gate for decisions: occasional confirmation that forces review where harm is most likely. This small friction can keep behavior in the safe regime while limiting burden. The best design is often none or minimal: either no extra step, or the smallest step that prevents the sudden jump. This provides practical guidance for product teams and regulators about when to require confirmation, logging, and choice preservation.</jats:p>
title: Delegation, Tipping, and Light-Touch Control in Consumer AI Agents: A Regime-Switching Theory of Misalignment

items.abstract: <jats:p>A user-facing AI agent does not merely answer questions; it may decide what to disclose, which service to choose, and how a person is represented to others. This shift exposes a gap in privacy and AI governance. Privacy policies and notice-and-consent regimes still treat personal data governance largely as disclosure control by individual users, while generative AI agents increasingly mediate decisions, permissions, recommendations, transactions, and reputational signals across platform ecosystems. This article develops a comparative policy analysis of three governance generations: P3P-style machine-readable privacy preferences, notice-and-consent/data protection regimes, and emerging user-facing generative AI agents. The central claim is that generative AI policy must move from privacy self-management to accountable delegation. Existing frameworks, including data protection, AI risk management, platform regulation, interoperability, and information-fiduciary approaches, provide partial tools for agent governance, but they do not fully address delegated authority, agent capture, generated reputational representations, or distributed responsibility. The analysis identifies personal AI agents as a distinct intermediary layer between individuals and platforms and proposes agent-specific extensions to existing frameworks: agent-readable obligations, bounded delegation, conflict controls, agent portability, auditable action logs, contestability, marketplace accountability, and public-interest transparency. The contribution is to reframe personal data governance as the regulation of infrastructures that act, decide, and negotiate in users&apos; names.</jats:p>
title: From Privacy Self-Management to Accountable Delegation: Policy Responses to User-Facing Generative AI Agents
